title: India Will Launch a Producer Price Index This Month. It Took Two Decades of Debate to Get Here.
excerpt: The new index will track services alongside goods for the first time, fundamentally changing how the world's fastest-growing major economy measures inflation at the production level
body:
After more than two decades of deliberation, India is finally replacing the wholesale price index as its primary measure of producer-level inflation. The government will launch a producer price index series this month, alongside a revamped WPI with a new base year — a shift that economists say will fundamentally change how India tracks, understands, and manages price movements across the economy.

## What Changes

The difference between WPI and PPI is not merely technical. India's wholesale price index covers only goods. The new producer price index will also capture services — a critical gap in an economy where services account for more than 55 per cent of GDP.

Praveen Mahto, principal economic adviser at the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, said the PPI data will include output PPI, input PPI, and service PPI covering seven services: banking, securities transactions, insurance, management of pension funds, railways, air passenger services, and telecom.

The Office of Economic Adviser under DPIIT will release the new WPI series, with 2022-23 as the base year, on June 15. The services PPI will be released quarterly, reflecting data availability and international practice.

## Why It Matters

The move brings India closer to international statistical standards followed by the United States, the European Union, Japan, and most OECD nations. The International Monetary Fund has long recommended that countries adopt PPI as a more accurate measure of production-side price pressures.

For policymakers, the distinction is consequential. WPI tracks prices at the wholesale level — essentially what producers receive for their goods. PPI tracks costs at the production level, including what producers pay for inputs. Over time, the PPI data will be used to strip inflation from real growth calculations, potentially changing how India's GDP growth rate itself is computed.

"The index will improve understanding of industry-specific inflation trends, support pricing decisions by businesses, and enable more targeted monetary and fiscal policies," economists familiar with the initiative said.

## The RBI Connection

The Reserve Bank of India uses the consumer price index as its primary inflation target, but WPI data has long served as a secondary reference for understanding supply-side price pressures. The addition of PPI — particularly the input PPI component — will give the central bank a more granular view of cost pressures before they reach consumers.

This matters acutely right now. With crude oil above $95 per barrel due to the Iran war, a weakening rupee, and a monsoon forecast revised down to just 90 per cent of the long-period average, India faces multiple simultaneous inflation pressures. A more precise measurement tool arrives at a moment when precision matters most.

## A Five-Year Transition

The government plans to transition from WPI to PPI over five years, though officials said the final timing will depend on how the new indices behave in practice. The measured approach reflects a recognition that decades of economic analysis, policy frameworks, and business decisions have been built around WPI data. Switching overnight would create discontinuities in time-series comparisons.

The seven initial services — banking, securities, insurance, pensions, railways, air travel, and telecom — represent sectors with relatively robust data infrastructure. The government is expected to expand coverage to additional services as data collection capacity improves.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRI investors monitoring India's economic fundamentals, the shift has practical implications. GDP deflator calculations — which determine whether India's nominal growth translates into real growth — will eventually incorporate PPI data. This could marginally alter reported growth rates, affecting how international investors and credit rating agencies assess the Indian economy.

More broadly, the PPI launch is a signal that India's statistical infrastructure is maturing. In a year when the country has negotiated the world's largest free trade deal with the EU, launched the world's largest digital payments system by transaction volume, and navigated a global energy crisis, the quiet modernisation of how it measures prices may be the reform that matters most over the long run.
author: Diaspora Desk
